features.claim: It was a giant pterosaur, the largest animal ever to fly.
features.quote: Quetzalcoatlus  is a genus of giant pterosaur, the largest animal ever to fly.

features.claim: It had an unusually long neck.
features.quote: Quetzalcoatlus had an unusually long neck, and when it stood on the ground it was as tall as a giraffe.

features.claim: When it stood on the ground it was as tall as a giraffe.
features.quote: Quetzalcoatlus had an unusually long neck, and when it stood on the ground it was as tall as a giraffe.

features.claim: It had a long beak with no teeth.
features.quote: The feeding habits of Quetzalcoatlus (which had a long beak with no teeth) are unknown.

features.claim: It was covered in hair-like filaments called pycnofibres.
features.quote: As a pterosaur, Quetzalcoatlus would have been covered in hair-like filaments called pycnofibres, and had extensive wing-membranes, which would have been distended by a long wing-finger.

features.claim: It had extensive wing-membranes stretched out by a long wing-finger.
features.quote: As a pterosaur, Quetzalcoatlus would have been covered in hair-like filaments called pycnofibres, and had extensive wing-membranes, which would have been distended by a long wing-finger.

features.claim: It likely walked on four legs.
features.quote: Based on the limb morphology of Q. lawsoni, related azhdarchids such as Zhejiangopterus, and pterosaurs at large, in addition to azhdarchid tracks from South Korea, Quetzalcoatlus was likely quadrupedal.

There have been various models of the morphology of pterodactyloid wings, though based on multiple well-preserved pterosaur specimens, it is likely that azhdarchids had broad wings, with a membrane called the brachiopatagium extending from the tip of the wing finger to the outer side of each ankle.

features.claim: It had a crest at the base of the beak.
features.quote: At the base of the beak, formed from the premaxilla, was a crest, referred to by some authors as a sagittal crest.
This contrasts the morphology seen in Q. lawsoni and other azhdarchids, which had small, narrow feet.

features.claim: It had a wingspan of 10 to 12 meters.
features.quote: The largest individuals measured a size of 10 to 12 meters wing-span (33-40 feet), but was light in construction (~200 pounds).

not_this.claim: It is wrong to picture it as a wading bird with large, broad feet, because it had small, narrow feet.
not_this.quote: However, wading animals tend to have large, long and broad feet, with a high surface area. This contrasts the morphology seen in Q. lawsoni and other azhdarchids, which had small, narrow feet.

debated.claim: Its exact size is hard to determine.
debated.quote: Quetzalcoatlus is regarded as one of the largest pterosaurs, though its exact size has been difficult to determine.

debated.claim: Its weight is uncertain, and the question cannot be settled at present.
debated.quote: Since we have only a few bones, the question of weight cannot be settled at present.

second_reading.quote: Like other pterosaurs, Quetzalcoatlus had light, hollow bones, supported internally by struts called trabeculae.

second_reading.claim: It is wrong to picture it as a fish-eating skimmer bird, because its jaw does not show the adaptations for skimming.
second_reading.quote: This view is gaining ground, because the jaw does not show the adaptations for skimming found in modern birds who catch fish this way.

second_reading.claim: It is wrong to picture it as a scavenger like a vulture, because its beak was weak and unhooked and could not tear flesh.
second_reading.quote: Since Q. lawsoni's beak was relatively weak and unhooked, being compared by Wann Langston Jr. to chopsticks, it is unlikely that it could have torn flesh from a carcass.

second_reading.claim: It is wrong to picture it as a skimmer, because azhdarchids lack the adaptations needed for skimming.
